context_blurb:
No two members of one species are exactly alike: they differ in size, colour, shape, speed and much else. These differences are variations. They matter because the world changes, and a storm, a drought or a new disease can turn a small difference into the one that decides who lives.

Many variations are inherited, carried in the genes that parents pass to their young. A paper strip soaked in a chemical called PTC reveals a hidden one: roughly three students in four find it bitter, and the others taste nothing. The difference lies in the genes each student inherited, above all one gene called TAS2R38. The whole tongue senses bitterness; the old map of taste zones is a myth.

Other variations come from the surroundings. A bigleaf hydrangea blooms blue in acid soil, where its roots can take up aluminium, and pink in alkaline soil, the opposite of acid, where they cannot. A cutting has the same genes as its parent bush, so if a blue bush's cutting blooms pink in a friend's garden, the soil in the friend's garden changed the colour. A difference made only by the surroundings is not passed on to the young.

Here is how a helpful variation spreads. Picture green and brown beetles on brown soil, where the green ones stand out to hungry birds. Fewer brown beetles are eaten, so more of them live to breed and pass their colour on, and since colour is inherited, their young are brown too. No beetle changes colour to suit the soil, and parents cannot give their young a colour because the young need it: the helpful variation must already be there.

In 2017 Colin Donihue's team had just measured the anole lizards on two islands of the Turks and Caicos when two hurricanes struck. Weeks later, the survivors' toe pads were bigger on average, and their bodies smaller, so the biggest had not done best. The biologists' best explanation was that lizards with bigger pads held on in the wind and lived, while the storms changed no lizard's feet. They could not rule out other causes, such as lizards blown in from another island. A year and a half later, lizards hatched since the storms had pads as big as the survivors'.

On a Galápagos island, a drought in 1977 left finches mostly big, hard seeds, which suit thick beaks, so thick-beaked birds came through best. Heavy rains from the end of 1982 then brought a flush of small, soft seeds. A thinner beak eats small seeds more efficiently, so after the rains the thin-beaked birds grew faster and raised the most young, and within a few years the average beak had shrunk. A variation that helps in one setting can hurt in another.

Cliff swallows often nest under highway bridges, where cars kill some of them. For thirty years in Nebraska, Charles Brown and Mary Bomberger Brown collected the road-killed birds, whose wings were a few millimetres longer than the rest. A shorter wing lets a swallow rise and swerve from a car faster, so short-winged birds lived to raise more young. Over those years the swallows' wings have grown shorter on average, and far fewer of the birds now die on the road. Charles Brown has said other causes may play a part too.

Variety can also carry a species through a disease. Ash dieback, caused by a fungus, has killed millions of ash trees across Europe, yet a few trees stay green among the dying. Those healthy trees inherited a resistance to the fungus, and their seedlings can inherit it from them. In one English wood, the young ash were already more resistant, on average, than the old. Resistance does not spread like a cold, and young trees without it die fastest.

A crop with no variety shows the danger. Until the 1950s, the Gros Michel was the banana on the ships to Europe and North America. Bananas are grown from shoots of older plants, not from seeds, so every Gros Michel was a copy of the same plant, with the same genes and the same weakness. Panama disease was neither new nor quick: its soil fungus creeps in through the roots and takes months to kill. Yet with no plant able to resist, it laid waste to vast tracts of plantations in Central America. Its successor, the Cavendish, resists that fungus, but it is a copy too, and a new strain now threatens it.
